matches.why: All twenty state P-01's mechanism: GET /invoices/:id binds req.params.id but never scopes the row to the caller (no owner_id predicate), and nearly all contrast it with the safe /receipts/:id which adds AND owner_id = $2. Line drift (R14 says 12, R106/R118/R125 say 7) is forgiven because the quoted handler is the same one. R30, R57 and R73 also mention absent authentication, but each one's evidence explicitly states the missing ownership check on /invoices/:id, so they are assigned here, to the mechanism they describe. Rejected near-misses: R52 puts BOLA on /receipts/:id, which is the SAFE counterpart that does filter by owner_id - its real complaint is JWT forgery, a different defect; R17, R82, R107 and R117 claim no authentication middleware is wired up anywhere (req.user may be undefined) - that is a different way the code goes wrong than the missing per-row owner scope, and R82's owner-check remark is a one-line aside behind a title and evidence wholly about middleware; R134 is about currentUser returning an undefined id.
matches.quote: GET /invoices/:id queries 'SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1' with only id parameter, no owner_id filter.

matches.why: All twenty-four name the same sink: req.query.order concatenated into `ORDER BY ${order}` in GET /invoices, with the note that the $1 bind protects the value but cannot bind a column. R26 (line 19), R113 (16), R124 (17), R123 (20) and R91 (20-23) misplace the line but quote the /invoices statement, so they are the same defect. Rejected near-misses: R19 and R39 point at /payments, the SAFE counterpart, whose column comes from the SORTABLE allowlist - they allege only that the allowlist might be extended carelessly in the future, which is a hypothetical about different code, not this defect.
matches.quote: The order variable from req.query.order is directly interpolated into the SQL string without parameterization.

matches.why: P-03 spans POST /branding/preview (accepts req.body.logoUrl) and fetchLogo (fetches it with redirect: 'follow' and no allowlist), so findings at either end are the same defect: R07, R47, R51, R88 and R96 sit on the route, the rest on lib/remote.js. R53, R90, R99, R111 and R129 frame it as the redirect-following half, which is the mechanism the defect names ('fetchLogo follows redirects with no allowlist'), so they are this defect and not a separate one. R111 also drags in fetchAsset's allowlist, but its evidence locates the flaw at 'Line 6 in fetchLogo()'. Rejected near-misses: R58 attacks fetchAsset - the SAFE counterpart, which parses the URL, checks ALLOWED and sets redirect: 'error' - alleging DNS rebinding against that allowlist, a different mechanism in different code; R16 is an unhandled promise rejection at the same line 38; R80 and R121 say /branding/preview lacks authentication, which is a missing-auth complaint, not the unvalidated outbound fetch.
matches.quote: Function fetchLogo() at line 6 uses fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }) allowing arbitrary redirect chains.

matches.why: All twenty-four state that currentUser calls jwt.decode without jwt.verify and no secret, so the signature is never checked and the sub/role claims are trusted. Several (R04, R23, R62, R75, R93, R94, R95, R98, R102, R112, R115, R119) additionally note the identical decode at line 12 in tagRequest; that is the same mechanism restated, so they still land here. R48, R75, R77 and R112 misplace the line to 4-5 without changing the mechanism. Rejected near-misses: R21, R41, R101 and R103 are about tagRequest returning req.session.user when no session middleware exists - dead code / undefined dereference, a different way that same file goes wrong (R103 mentions the unverified JWT only as a cross-reference to a separate finding of its own); R134 is about currentUser yielding {id: undefined} for a missing token and downstream falsy checks, a null-handling defect, not signature verification; R116 is a dependency-version guess about node-fetch.
matches.quote: The code uses jwt.decode() which only decodes the JWT payload without verifying the signature.

matches.why:
Every lib/render.js finding describes the same sink: invoiceNote interpolates note into `
${note}
` with no escaping, and most contrast it with the safe customerName, which does call escapeHtml. Labels vary (reflected vs stored vs HTML injection) and severities range from medium to high, but the mechanism stated is identical, so the variation is understated severity, not a different defect. R110 slips by saying footer also uses escapeHtml (it uses Number), which does not change the defect it reports. No finding in this file blamed customerName or footer, so there was no safe-counterpart false positive to reject here.
matches.quote: The `note` parameter is interpolated directly into an HTML string without escaping.
